reviews.review: Short loverly game! The story keeps you hooked on as it develops, UI is well made and fits the genre perfectly. If you liked HackNet or Uplink, you'll probably enjoy this little detective story as well.

The game play felt similar to some elements of papers please, but now in an investigative stand point to solve a series of crimes. Overall this has so much potential to be REALLY GOOD, the gameplay elements was very immersive and FUN and I can see myself sinking in my life to a game like this if they had an endless mode. For cons, it is a short game and I wish they had more filler or side content to add to the gameplay and not only focus on the story. I also was a little disappointed that there are no multiple endings and most actions you do will not really matter in the long run, which seems like a missed opportunity IMO.

Honestly, no matter what anyone says, this is a masterpiece. 

Yes, the plot was a bit predictable, but that didn't stop me from having a really great time playing this game.
The puzzles are interesting, although the one about Tanner's house was rather obscure. It's a shame the game didn't fully tell the story, but I'm eagerly awaiting The Operator 2, which hopefully will address all the shortcomings of the first.  

Highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys this type of games!!

Right as you start to find your footing in the game and really get into the story, it ends. I was shocked at how little gameplay there is (especially for how expensive the game is). The ending was depressing and kind of open ended, so it feels like you never really get any closure on the story. The format of the game was really interesting, and I enjoyed the storyline, but the positives unfortunately do not outweigh the negatives in this case.

If you are looking for a captivating interactive movie or story for a lazy night, I would absolutely recommend this game. It's atmospheric, the voice acting is good, and the method of delivery is super cool. 

And I wish there was a sort of middle recommendation. I really enjoyed it, and...

If you're looking for a longer game where you actually have to problem solve on your own, I'd pass on this one. Like many other reviews mention, its very much click here, and then there. There were a few moments where all you did was act as a middle man in a way that's not very rewarding. 

I would have liked it if this was a collection of several cases, with different leads you could follow on your own, or a larger story that takes more time to complete. I was so disappointed to have such cool tools given to me... only to use them once and never touch it again. 

And unfortunately, given the very linear story and no alternative routes, the abrupt ending ultimately knocked the wind from my sails real quick. I think it also could have been improved with more dust to sift through, as the twist wasn't that much of a shock unfortunately. 

That all being said, if the sequel they teased is a lot longer, more sprawling, and less linear, I would absolutely pick it up. Despite my ultimate disappointment, I really enjoyed it up until the end, I just wish there was more. 

Ultimately, since my complaint is I wish there was more, and because I think the quality is good, I recommend it. As long as you expect more of a visual novel experience, and less something like Shadow of Doubt.

The Operator offers a remarkably engaging narrative experience, supported by a strong storyline and a well-executed plot twist. The structure of each case is thoughtfully designed: from the call system to the investigative tasks, every step feels purposeful and polished. Working through evidence, analyzing data, and piecing together conclusions is consistently satisfying and stands out as one of the game’s greatest strengths.

Because the investigative tools and the workstation interface are so enjoyable to use, I found myself wishing for a mode that would provide long-term engagement beyond the main story. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once it ends, the gameplay loop—despite being excellent—comes to an abrupt stop.

A dedicated free-play or “ongoing operations” mode could meaningfully extend the game’s lifespan. For example, players could receive procedurally generated cases or scenario-based assignments that scale in complexity, allowing them to continue applying the tools and systems introduced in the main storyline. This would give players who enjoy the investigative process a space to keep refining their skills and exploring the mechanics without a fixed ending.

I am very much looking forward to The Operator 2, and I genuinely believe that adding an optional long-term mode—whether free-play, case generator, or rotating scenario board—would significantly enhance replay value and increase the game’s overall appeal.

For anyone considering this title: the core experience is absolutely worth it, and the investigative gameplay is exceptionally well-crafted. The story alone justifies the €14 price, and I can recommend it without hesitation.

I wanted to love this game but I just cannot recommend you spend money on what is ultimately a disappointing experience. 

The game has a great concept with a strong atmosphere, and what I hoped was great potential but the overall experience ends up feeling disappointingly thin. Reading reviews and looking at the blurb I felt that I was promised tension, deduction, and deeper problem-solving. Unfortunately, it never fully delivers on that potential.

The biggest issue is simply its length. Just as the mechanics start to click and the world begins to feel intriguing, the game is over. It ends before it can build momentum or explore its own ideas in any meaningful way. What could have been a gripping investigation feels more like the prologue to a larger game that never arrives.

The story also ends up predictable. Key beats begin to telegraph themselves early, and the ending lands exactly where you expect it to. Without twists, red herrings, or layers to peel back, the narrative lacks the depth needed to keep you engaged or surprised.

The investigations themselves feel shallow as well. Each case presents a problem, but they’re often solved with just a few simple steps. There’s rarely a need to dig deeper, only once or twice was I cross-referencing clues, or genuinely thinking like an investigator. Instead of complex puzzles or branching deductions, you get straightforward tasks that resolve too quickly to be satisfying.

Overall, The Operator is an interesting idea wrapped in a very short, very predictable package. If you’re looking for a brief atmospheric diversion, it works—but if you want a substantial investigative experience, this one doesn’t reach far enough.

I absolutely love this game’s design and idea but sadly I don't think it was executed very well.

Rather than feeling in control of the narrative, most of the game was spent watching the story unfold with little player-contribution. There were different options to choose during conversations, which would somewhat influence the story plot-wise, but given that it's a mystery game and the choice of options available were very limited and surface-level (e.g. will you lie or not lie), replaying it to see what else (if anything) could have happened doesn't feel worth my time.

The story had some small unexpected and exciting twists, however most of these developments were overshadowed by the main plot being very predictable. I think if they had delved more into the individual cases within the game itself and focused less on forming an overarching plot, it would have been much more enjoyable.

The nature of the game put it in a great position to deliver really varied and unique puzzles (e.g. code breaking, crime solving, hacking -- all of which were very fun), yet the quantity of puzzles was seriously lacking. It felt like maybe only an hour out of the 3.5 hours of time spent playing was actually focused on problem-solving and the rest was in tedious over-explanatory conversation. 

I understand this is tagged with visual novel and so maybe the developers intended it for it to be more of a narrative-based experience, but if that is the reason for the lack of puzzles, I would have expected the plot to be more developed and have less of an obvious ending.

Things to know: 

1: The story is linear. However, it's a good story, so you won't really care.
2: No re-playability (unless you really want to just grab any achievement you may have missed, but otherwise no point to playing it more than once) . However, not all games need re-playability to be fully worth the cost. 
3: it is a short game. it took me about 4 hours to beat it and that was me taking my time and looking at everything. 

Summary: in this game, you feel as though you are playing a main role in a cat and mouse police thriller movie. It is NOT horror, but it IS suspenseful.  And when I say playing a character in a movie-I mean just that. not playing a character in a game like a movie, but a real "This is you, this is your job, this is what you are having to face" feel to it that really pulls you in. While the main plot isn't unique, the slight twists especially at the very end and the variations they used to tell this main story make it a stand out game.  if you loved movies like face off or silences of the lambs or anything along those lines, you absolutely will enjoy this game. cheaper than going to an actual movie theatre  and for something that will last you twice as long as a standard movie.  

This is definitely one of the best games of this style I have ever seen or played, and i highly recommend it. given some of the puzzles, I would say this game is definitely better suited to adult gamers, but anyone with the intelligence and patience for such things would probably really enjoy this IF they enjoy cat and mouse thriller movies.  

Also as a bonus: Due to the style it is made in, you do NOT need a top of the line computer or anywhere near close to it to play it. So if you have a dirt cheap PC from say the last 5 years?  Chances are it will run absolutely fine and with no need to change any settings. I am running on a rig almost 3 generations behind at this point, and had zero issues with this game. 

It also looks like the developers are working on a sequel to this game. Unknown if that will continue further into this story or be a new one entirely, but if they  keep the save high level of story telling and suspense I have no doubt it will also be amazing.   

I honestly didn't have to many hopes when going into this game, but for once I was absolutely amazed at what I actually got. So if you can get it either at full price or on sale, I definitely recommend it. just don't go into it thinking its going to be a hundreds of hours or infinite re-playability game and you should have no problems either.

PROS, but:
All elements of the game could be built towards a randomized investigative type game (look at "Papers, please" or the game described below and then apply the principles to this type of game play).  
Bomb-defusal mini-game was innovative and tense, could have multiple scenarios play out.

A similar type of game that accomplished this was Sid Meier's Covert Operations. If the type of game-play "The Operator" presents is what you're looking for and you can stomach very retro gaming (this was an DOS era game), would recommend checking out Covert Operations instead.

But again, the story is compelling. Will look to see if the sequel's gaming experience expands in a way I was hoping this game would play out: not as a movie, but a game where the player has actual agency in the world.

To the Devs:
You have a lot of components in hand to assemble a compelling, unique "radiant" type investigative game with an engaging story (or stories) lying beneath the surface to draw the player into the game's world. Looking forward with cautious optimism to see how the sequel(s) plays out.

To simplify (somewhat) integrating multiple endings (and this doesn't have to be visible to the players, or could be some sort of end of day report/summary), continue with the the day to day system, and use the day end to grade the player's actions and, using key flagged actions (as a suggestion: timing when completed could affect endings too - in time, late, way too late, done wrong, etc), lead them towards whatever multiple endings are created in the next (probably third) game.

It's an interesting game and I enjoyed playing a bit of it, but the developer has a specific idea in mind about how it is to be played and I'm not into that.  Specifically, when listening to an audio file, the controls are locked and you can't do anything else.  The developer has said that he wants to be able to focus the player's attention, but that's not how my attention works and it's very uncomfortable.  Instead of focusing my intention, it's like someone powered up a megaphone next to my ear and is shouting, "this is all artificial!  Stop being immersed!  This is a video game!  The stakes are very low because none of this is real!"

The ideal situation for me would be being able to replay all of the audios - including recordings of the "real time" conversations - repeatedly while I peruse the visual and text data.  This is how I have investigated things in the past (though those were technical investigations and not criminal investigations): get everything in front of me and let my mind chew on a bunch of it at once to get into it.

I'm not exactly normal when it comes to my focus and attention, but the make or break question for Steam reviews is, "would I recommend this?"  In this case, I don't.

UPDATE: I'm not suggesting that the dev should change the game to suit me; I'm just saying that I don't recommend it.

I really enjoyed the style of investigation and the way the story was unfolding piece by piece. However, the ending fell flat and painted my overall opinion as negative. None of your actions mattered in any shape or form, there is really only one ending to be had. The choices are just an illusion, all paths lead to the same end. I guess some people like it, but for me this immediately detached all the emotion I had invested to the game and the characters and it felt like I had waisted all that time trying to choose the right path. 

A lot of strings were also left loose, and while it may have been to tease a sequel, it did not feel satisfying. A good game should be it's own complete piece that can enjoyed without digging through a Discord server for additional info or waiting for a sequel to explain everything. 

Another grievance I have with the game lies in the save system; you can't manually save and it only happens automatically at certain checkpoints. This feels extremely outdated and forces you to either play for an unknown amount of time until you hit a checkpoint, or you have to keep starting the day over because your progress isn't saved. Just give people the option to save manually and reload from a checkpoint if they have forgotten what happened. I had to take a 10 month break from the game because the save system made playing feel like a chore - you can't just play for a few minutes (or however long you feel like playing) at a time because your progress could be all for nothing.

I think the game and the developer have a lot of potential and I believe that if the second game fixes all these issues, it can be GREAT.
